When edge 5 is none, edge 4 is the only route from the intermediate nodes to the output, so removing it is much more harmful.
If edge 4 is none, node 1 reaches the output only through edge 2 (often also none), so improving edge 0 has little or no downstream effect.

Edge 2 feeds node 2, which is dead when edge 5 is none, so the conv added there has no effect on the output.

Removing the input-to-output residual hurts trainability much more than removing a conv or pool on that edge.
When edge 0 is none, node 1 carries zero features, so a skip from node 1 to the output contributes nothing.
In pooling-dominated cells with no learnable ops, adding a 3x3 conv supplies much-needed capacity, so the gain is larger than in conv-rich cells.

These hypotheses come from prior knowledge of NAS-Bench-201 and from the cell's structure, not from the 100 experiments, whose results aren't available. Most of them rest on one idea. When a 'none' edge cuts a node off from the output, edits upstream of that node lose their effect. When an edit removes the last remaining route to the output, the result is a collapse. A second, smaller group concerns the direct 0→3 edge: a skip connection there is far more valuable than a convolution in the same place.
